L22: # Understanding cite13†SC 1.4.11†w3.org Non-text Contrast (Level AA)
L23: ## In Brief
L24: 
L25: Goal
L26:     Important visual information meets the same minimum contrast required for larger text.
L27: What to do
L28:     Ensure meaningful visual cues achieve 3:1 against the background.
L29: Why it's important
L30:     Some people cannot see elements with low contrast.
L31: ## Success Criterion (SC)
L32: 
L33: The visual cite14†presentation of the following have a cite15†contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s):
L34: User Interface Components
L35:     Visual information required to identify cite16†user interface components and cite17†states , except for inactive components or where the appearance of the component is determined by the cite18†user agent and not modified by the author;
L36: Graphical Objects
L37:     Parts of graphics required to understand the content, except when a particular presentation of graphics is cite19†essential to the information being conveyed.
L38: ## Intent
L39: 
L40: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that user interface components (i.e., controls) and meaningful graphics are distinguishable by people with moderately low vision. The requirements and rationale are similar to those for large text in cite20†1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) . Note that this requirement does not apply to inactive user interface components.
L41: Low contrast controls are more difficult to perceive, and may be completely missed by people with a visual impairment. Similarly, if a graphic is needed to understand the content or functionality of the web page then it should be perceivable by people with low vision or other impairments without the need for contrast-enhancing assistive technology.
L42: 
L43: Note
L44: The 3:1 contrast ratios referenced in this success criterion is intended to be treated as threshold values. When comparing the computed contrast ratio to the success criterion ratio, the computed values should not be rounded (e.g. 2.999:1 would not meet the 3:1 threshold).
L45: 
L46: Note
L47: Because authors do not have control over user settings for font smoothing and anti-aliasing, when evaluating this Success Criterion, refer to the colors obtained from the user agent, or the underlying markup and stylesheets, rather than the non-text elements as presented on screen.
L48: Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin lines and shapes of non-text elements may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter color than the actual color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where non-text elements have a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but have a much lower contrast in practice.
L49: In these cases, best practice would be for authors to avoid particularly thin lines and shapes, or to use a combination of colors that exceeds the normative requirements of this success criterion.
L50: ### User Interface Components
L51: 
L52: Unless the control is inactive, any visual information provided that is necessary for a user to identify that a control is present and how to operate it must have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio with the adjacent colors. Also, any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.
L53: This success criterion does not require that changes in color that differentiate between states of an individual component meet the 3:1 contrast ratio when they do not appear next to each other. For example, there is not a new requirement that visited links contrast with the default color, or that mouse hover indicators contrast with the default state.
L54: However, the component must not lose contrast with the adjacent colors, and non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.
L55: #### Boundaries
L56: This success criterion does not require that controls have a visual boundary indicating the hit area. If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements.
L57: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.
L58: Note
L59: 
L60: Even when a control does not need to have a visual boundary indicating its hit area, it will still need to have a sufficiently contrasting focus indication.
L61: 
L62: Note
L63: 
L64: For people with cognitive disabilities, it is a best practice to delineate the boundary of all controls, even those that have visible content, to aid in the recognition of controls and the completion of activities.
L65: Figure 1. Pass: A button without a visual boundary – the button's text is sufficient to indicate the presence of the control. The same button, when focused, still has a sufficiently contrasting focus indicator (grey `#949494` against white, with a contrast ratio of 3:1).
L66: #### Adjacent colors
L67: 
L68: For user interface components 'adjacent colors' means the colors adjacent to the component. For example, if an input has a white internal background, dark border, and white external background the 'adjacent color' to the component would be the white external background.
L69: 
L70: Figure 2. Pass: A standard text input with a grey border (`#767676`) and white adjacent color outside the component
L71: If components use several colors, any color which does not interfere with identifying the component can be ignored for the purpose of measuring contrast ratio. For example, a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness (perceived luminance).
L72: The following example shows an input that has a light background on the inside and a dark background around it. The input also has a dark grey border which is considered to be subsumed into the dark background. The border does not interfere with identifying the component, so the contrast ratio is taken between the white background and dark blue background.
L73: Figure 3. Pass: The contrast of the input background (white) and color adjacent to the control (dark blue `#003366`) is sufficient. There is also a border (silver) on the component that is not required to contrast with either.
L74: 
L75: For visual information required to identify a state, such as the check in a checkbox or the thumb of a slider, that part might be within the component so the adjacent color might be another part of the component.
L76: Figure 4. Pass: A customized checkbox with light grey check (`#E5E5E5`), which has a contrast ratio of 5.6:1 with the purple box (`#6221EA`).
L77: 
L78: It is possible to use a flat design where the status indicator fills the component and does not contrast with the component, but does contrast with the colors adjacent to the component.
L79: Figure 5. Pass: The first radio button shows the default state with a grey (`#949494`) circle. The second and third show the radio button selected and filled with a color that contrasts with the color adjacent to the component. The last example shows the state indicator contrasting with the component colors.
L80: #### Relationship with Use of Color
L81: The cite21†Use of Color success criterion addresses changing only the color (hue) of an object or text without otherwise altering the object's form. The principle is that contrast ratio (the difference in brightness) can be used to distinguish text or graphics. For example, cite22†G183: Using a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 to distinguish inline text links from surrounding text is a technique to use a contrast ratio of 3:1 with surrounding text to distinguish links and controls.
L82: In that case the Working Group regards a link color that meets the 3:1 contrast ratio relative to the non-linked text color as satisfying the Success Criterion cite21†1.4.1 Use of color since it is relying on contrast ratio as well as color (hue) to convey that the text is a link.
L83: Non-text information within controls that uses a change of hue alone to convey the value or state of an input, such as a 1-5 star indicator with a black outline for each star filled with either yellow (full) or white (empty) is likely to fail the Use of color criterion rather than this one.
L84: 
L85: Figure 6. Pass: Two examples which pass this success criterion, using either a solid fill to indicate a checked-state that has contrast, or a thicker border as well as yellow fill.
L86: Figure 7. Fail: The first example fails the Use of color criterion due to relying on yellow and white hues. The second example fails the Non-text contrast criterion due to the yellow (`#FFF000`) to white contrast ratio of 1.2:1.
L87: 
L88: Using a change of contrast for focus and other states is a technique to differentiate the states. This is the basis for cite23†G195: Using an author-supplied, visible focus indicator , and more techniques are being added.
L89: #### Relationship with Focus Visible
L90: 
L91: In combination with cite24†2.4.7 Focus Visible , the visual focus indicator for a component must have sufficient contrast against the adjacent background when the component is focused, except where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author.
L92: 
L93: Most focus indicators appear outside the component - in that case it needs to contrast with the background that the component is on. Other cases include focus indicators which are:
L94:   * only inside the component and need to contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component.
L95:   * the border of the component (inside the component and adjacent to the outside) and need to contrast with both adjacent colors.
L96:   * partly inside and partly outside, where either part of the focus indicator can contrast with the adjacent colors.
L97: 
L98: Figure 8. Pass: The internal yellow indicator (`#FFFF00`) contrasts with the blue button background (`#4189B9`).
L99: Figure 9. Fail: The external yellow indicator (`#FFFF00`) does not contrast with the white background (`#FFF`) which the component is on.
L100: Figure 10. Pass: The external green indicator (`#008000`) does contrast with the white background (`#FFF`) which the component is on. It does not need to contrast with both the component background and the component, as visually the effect is that the button is noticeably larger, and it's not necessary for a user to be able to discern this extra border in isolation. Although this passes non-text contrast, it is not a good indicator unless it is very thick.
L101: New in WCAG 2.2: There is a AAA criterion in WCAG 2.2 that addresses this aspect, cite25†Focus Appearance .
L102: If an indicator is partly inside and partly outside the component, either part of the indicator could provide contrast.
L103: 
L104: Figure 11. Pass: The focus indicator is partially inside, partially outside the button. The internal part of the yellow indicator (`#FFFF00`) contrasts with the blue button background (`#4189B9`).
L105: If the focus indicator changes the border of the component within the visible boundary it must contrast with the component. Typically an outline goes around (outside) the visible boundary of the component, in this case changing the border is just inside the visible edge of the component.
L106: 
L107: Figure 12. Fail: The border of the control changes from blue (`#4189B9`) to green (`#4B933A`). This is within the component and does not contrast with the inside background of the component.
L108: Figure 13. Fail: An inner border of dark green (`#008000`) does contrast with the black border, but does not contrast with the blue component background.
L109: 
L110: Figure 14. Pass: An inner border of white contrasts with the black border and the blue component background.
L111: Note that this success criterion does not directly compare the focused and unfocused states of a control - if the focus state relies on a change of color (e.g., changing only the background color of a button), this success criterion does not define any requirement for the difference in contrast between the two states.
L112: 
L113: Figure 15. Not in scope: The change of background within the component is not in scope of non-text contrast. However, this would not pass cite26†Use of color .
L114: #### Hover states
L115: The language of Non-text Contrast specifically calls out "visual information required to identify...states." When users talk about a hover state, they are normally referring to a visual effect that takes place when the pointer is positioned over a control. However, there are a number of HTML components (such as buttons, checkboxes, radio buttons, and selects) which do not by default display any additional visual effects when the user moves a pointer control over them.
L116: The pointer itself, via its location, is the indicator of whether the user is hovering on a component. Therefore, additional author-supplied visual treatments for hover are not "required to identify" the hover state. Those treatments can be considered supplemental and do not themselves need to contrast 3:1 against the background.
L117: This is not to say that other hover effects are discouraged. For instance, some native components alter the shape of the pointer when it is hovering over a control; the pointer becomes an I-beam when it hovers over text inputs and text areas. There will be cases where some users may benefit from additional visual hover effects, such as bolding text or use of drop shadows. However, other users may find strong hover effects distracting.
L118: The key consideration for any hover effect is that it does not cause a component itself to lose sufficient contrast against adjacent colors, or cause the visual indicators for other states, such as focus or selection, to lose sufficient contrast.
L119: #### Inactive User Interface Components
L120: 
L121: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable. An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.
L122: 
L123: Figure 16. An inactive button using default browser styles
L124: Inactive components, such as disabled controls in HTML, are not available for user interaction. The decision to exempt inactive controls from the contrast requirements was based on a number of considerations. Although it would be beneficial to some people to discern inactive controls, a one-size-fits-all solution has been very difficult to establish.
L125: A method of varying the presentation of disabled controls, such as adding an icon for disabled controls, based on user preferences is anticipated as an advancement in the future.
L126: ### Graphical Objects
L127: 
L128: The term "graphical object" applies to stand-alone icons such as a print icon (with no text), and the important parts of a more complex diagram such as each line in a graph. For simple graphics such as single-color icons the entire image is a graphical object. Images made up of multiple lines, colors and shapes will be made of multiple graphical objects, some of which are required for understanding.
L129: Not every graphical object needs to contrast with its surroundings - only those that are required for a user to understand what the graphic is conveying. cite27†Gestalt principles†en.wikipedia.org such as the "law of continuity" can be used to ignore minor overlaps with other graphical objects or colors.
L130: 
L131: cite28†Image: An orange circle with a white telephone icon in the middle. L132: Figure 17. The phone icon is a simple shape within the orange (`#E3660E`) circle. The meaning can be understood from that icon alone, the background behind the circle is irrelevant. The orange background and the white icon have a contrast ratio greater than 3:1, which passes.
L133: 
L134: The graphical object is the white phone icon.
L135: 
L136: cite29†Image: A red magnet with grey tips and a black outline. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is a sensible polish plan. I’d make these six adjustments before implementation:

1. **Fix focus contrast on the brown bar.** The existing blue focus ring against `#41220c` has approximately **2.1:1 contrast**, below the 3:1 requirement for a custom focus indicator. Use a white or two-color ring on the bar. Checking text contrast alone misses this. [Plan location](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:192) · [WCAG guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html)

2. **Correct the mobile keyboard expectations.** With Back followed by Show more in the bar, Shift+Tab from the details heading reaches **Show more first**, then Back. The stated keyboard walk will fail on mobile. Keep the logical DOM order and update the acceptance test accordingly. [Plan location](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:74)

3. **Test the camera fix during an already-running zoom.** `animate: false` addresses the described repeated-fit problem, but Leaflet checks `_animatingZoom` before that option and can still discard requests during an existing zoom. Add rapid zoom → Recenter and select → Back checks, ensuring the latest requested view is applied after animation finishes. [Plan location](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:88) · [Leaflet source](https://github.com/Leaflet/Leaflet/blob/v1.9.4/src/map/Map.js#L1659-L1667)

4. **Make the compact summary respond to panel width.** A viewport breakpoint below 360px won’t protect a narrow desktop sidebar. Use a container query or a layout that stacks when its own available width is insufficient. Test long addresses and enlarged text; the fixed 112px thumbnail competes with the existing two-column definition list. [Plan location](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:156)

5. **Hide the entire decorative thumbnail from assistive technology.** Empty image alt text is appropriate, but `ParkImage` also renders visible “No image available” text on failure. That duplicate placeholder remains accessible despite `alt=""`. Put `aria-hidden="true"` on the decorative thumbnail component; keep gallery images accessible. [Plan location](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:145)

6. **Include these Codex reviews in the submission logs.** Exporting only Claude’s project logs omits another AI tool used for the exercise. Include full Codex conversations and verify delegated sessions are included too. The brief requires logs from every tool used. [Export step](/Users/tom/.claude/plans/handoffs-handoff-7-md-pasted-content-id-rustling-sunbeam.md:249) · :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/tom/park-finder/docs/local-parks-candidate.pdf" purpose="source"}
